SEOUL, South Korea (CNN)  -- South Korea will open its market to most U.S. beef, a senior government official said Thursday, according to state media. Thousands of people have taken to the streets of the South Korean capital in protest at the deal . South Korea banned imports of U.S. beef in 2003 amid concerns over a case of mad cow disease in the United States. The ban closed what was then the third-largest market for U.S. beef exporters. It resumed limited imports last year -- allowing boneless beef from cattle under 30 months of age -- but that re-opening was subject to interruptions and closed altogether in October 2007. A deal that South Korea and the United States struck last month bans the import of high-risk materials, like tonsils, brains, spinal cord marrow and a section of the small intestine, Agriculture Minister Chung Woon-chun said Thursday, according to South Korea's Yonhap news agency. These parts pose the greatest risk of transmitting mad cow disease to humans. The ban will be lifted within a few days, once the government's new import rules have been published. The pending resumption of U.S. beef imports hasn't been without political costs for President Lee Myung-bak. He apologized to the nation last week for failing to fully understand concerns about mad cow disease. In downtown Seoul, thousands of people have regularly staged protests, chanting "We don't want crazy cows," since the deal to revive beef imports was announced. And the main opposition party has taken up the fight. "We will be forced to make a critical decision if the government pushes through its plan to announce resumption of beef imports," said Sohn Hak-kyu, leader of the main opposition United Democratic Party, Yonhap reported. "If the government and the ruling party ignore this warning, we will come up with every possible measure to stop them." The opposition has already filed a suit to suspend implementation of new beef import terms, according to Yonhap. Lee's ruling Grand National Party (GNP) is working to soothe tensions, saying that American beef is safe to eat and that adequate safety precautions have been taken. "The government has tried its best to free the public from unnecessary concerns, and sufficient countermeasures have been prepared," said Lee Hahn-koo, the party's chief policymaker, Yonhap reported. When South Korea and the United States reached the deal in April to re-open the South Korean market, they removed the major obstacle to U.S. congressional approval of the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement (FTA). Lee urged the National Assembly this month to ratify the agreement as soon as possible to provide fresh impetus to the sluggish Korean economy, saying it will create 300,000 jobs. But the opposition has promised to fight the FTA until the beef pact is nullified. In 2003, the United States exported $815 million pounds of beef and beef variety meats to South Korea. The U.S. beef industry has lost up to $4 billion since the market closed, according to the U.S. Meat Export Federation.

**South Korea to Reopen Market to Most U.S. Beef Imports, Easing Long-Running Trade Dispute**

*Seoul/Washington* — South Korea has agreed to allow most American beef back into the country, marking a major step toward resolving one of the most sensitive trade disputes between Seoul and Washington and reopening what was once one of the most lucrative overseas markets for U.S. cattle producers.

The decision follows years of restrictions imposed after the discovery of bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or BSE — commonly known as mad cow disease — in the United States in 2003. South Korea, previously a leading buyer of American beef, halted imports at the time amid concerns that infected beef products could pose risks to human health.

Under the new arrangement, South Korea will permit a broad range of U.S. beef shipments, subject to safeguards intended to address public health concerns. The agreement is expected to cover most beef products from American cattle, though specific rules may continue to apply to parts considered higher risk, such as certain brain, spinal cord or nerve tissues associated with BSE transmission.

### A ban rooted in mad cow fears

South Korea banned U.S. beef in December 2003 after the first U.S. case of mad cow disease was confirmed in Washington state. The disease affects cattle and has been linked in humans to variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a rare but fatal neurological disorder believed to be caused by consumption of contaminated tissues from infected animals.

Although international animal-health authorities later classified the United States as a controlled-risk country and U.S. officials argued that American inspection and feed-control systems made the beef supply safe, South Korean consumers remained wary. Beef imports became a politically charged issue, tied not only to food safety but also to perceptions of government transparency and the balance of power in the U.S.-South Korea alliance.

Partial reopenings in previous years were repeatedly interrupted by disputes over bone fragments, inspection standards and the age of cattle eligible for export. South Korea had at times allowed only boneless beef from younger cattle, reflecting concerns that BSE risk increases with age and that bone-in products could include higher-risk material.

### Public health concerns remain politically potent

South Korean officials said the latest decision is based on scientific assessments and international standards, but public health concerns are likely to remain a focus of opposition parties, civic groups and consumer organizations. Critics have argued that imported beef should be subject to strict age limits and comprehensive inspection rules, particularly because BSE has a long incubation period and cannot be detected through routine visual inspection.

Supporters of the reopening say the risk to consumers is extremely low when specified risk materials are removed and feed restrictions are enforced. They also argue that continued restrictions were increasingly difficult to justify under global trade rules and could complicate broader economic ties with the United States.

The issue has broader diplomatic significance. Washington has long pressed Seoul to reopen its market, and U.S. beef access has been closely linked to congressional and political support for deeper trade relations, including the U.S.-South Korea free trade agenda.

### Heavy losses for U.S. beef exporters

For the U.S. beef industry, South Korea’s ban was costly. Before the 2003 halt, South Korea was one of the top foreign markets for American beef, buying hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth annually. Industry estimates have placed losses from the closure in the billions of dollars over the years, including lost sales, reduced market share and the cost of rebuilding consumer confidence.

In 2003, U.S. beef exports to South Korea were valued at roughly **$800 million**, making it the third-largest export destination for American beef at the time. After the ban, shipments collapsed, and competitors such as Australia and New Zealand gained ground in the Korean market. U.S. cattle producers and meatpackers have argued that regaining access is essential to restoring export growth, especially as overseas demand plays an increasingly important role in supporting beef prices.

The reopening is expected to benefit U.S. ranchers, meat processors and exporters, though analysts caution that sales may recover gradually. South Korean consumers may remain cautious, and retailers could face pressure over labeling and sourcing. Still, American beef is likely to regain market share because of its competitive price and popularity among restaurants and consumers before the ban.

### Trade and politics intertwined

The decision highlights the intersection of food safety, domestic politics and international trade. For South Korea, reopening the market may strengthen ties with Washington and help advance broader economic cooperation. For the United States, it represents a long-sought victory for agricultural exporters and a sign that science-based trade standards can overcome politically sensitive barriers.

But the issue is unlikely to disappear entirely. Any future BSE case in North America, or any shipment found to violate Korean import rules, could reignite public concern and political opposition. Both governments are expected to emphasize inspection procedures, traceability and removal of high-risk materials as they seek to reassure consumers and stabilize trade.

For now, the agreement offers the U.S. beef industry its best opportunity in years to recover a market it lost almost overnight — and gives South Korea’s government the task of convincing the public that renewed imports can be managed safely.
